items: No index = COLLSCAN: every document read for one query.
Index = ordered keys plus a `RecordId` pointer to the doc.
MongoDB indexes are WiredTiger row-store B-trees, O(log n).
`_id` index is automatic, unique, and cannot be dropped.
Descend the tree, land on the first matching key, walk in order.
Sorted keys serve equality, range and sort from one index.
`$gt`, `$lt`, `$gte`, `$lte` are contiguous slices of the tree.
Indexes are per-collection; one index per predicate branch.
Costs disk and RAM in the WiredTiger cache.
Slows every insert, update, delete touching indexed fields.
10 indexes = 11 B-tree writes for one insert.
Write amplification grows with each index you add.

blocks.title: Sort Memory Cap
blocks.text: In-memory sorts are capped at 100 MB and abort with `Sort exceeded memory limit`. An index in the sort order removes the SORT stage entirely.

blocks.title: Building Live
items: Hybrid build yields to readers and writers.
Still saturates disk I/O — schedule it.
Start with `db.coll.createIndex({field: 1})`.

lines: // every document contributes exactly one key

items: Direction is irrelevant here: the tree walks backwards fine.
`{age:1}` serves `sort({age:1})` and `sort({age:-1})`.
Serves equality `{age:30}` and range `{age:{$gte:18,$lt:65}}`.
`$in` becomes a bounded multi-interval index scan.
A document missing the field still gets a `null` key.
`{age: null}` matches missing and explicitly-null docs alike.
`createIndex({address:1})` indexes the whole subdocument.
Whole-object equality only, and inner field order matters.

blocks.title: Selectivity Wins
blocks.text: An index on a boolean `isActive` split 50/50 rarely beats a collection scan. Index the fields that cut the candidate set hard.

left.title: sparse
items: Skips docs lacking the field
Smaller index
Cannot answer `{f: null}`
Cannot serve a full sort

right.title: partial
items: Arbitrary predicate filter
Query must be a provable subset
Modern replacement
Pairs with `unique`

blocks.title: Housekeeping
items: `{hidden:true}`: maintained but invisible to the planner.
Test a drop safely, unhide instantly if latency regresses.
Auto name `age_1`; pass `{name:'idx_age'}` under 127 bytes.

lines: // hard ceiling: 32 fields per compound index

items: Keys sort lexicographically by the tuple, left to right.
All `status` values group; inside each, `createdAt` descending.
Only the leading contiguous subset can be seeked.
No leading `a` means no start point in the tree.
`{a,b,c}` makes `{a}` and `{a,b}` redundant — drop them.
Equality first, then Sort fields, then Range fields.
Equality pins one contiguous slice of the tree.
A range opens the slice; fields after it lose sorted order.

blocks.title: Wrong Order Still Runs
blocks.text: The index keeps filtering, but explain grows a `stage: 'SORT'` — a blocking sort bolted onto the scan. Check for it before shipping.

items: Every field read and returned lives inside the index.
Needs `_id: 0` in the projection unless `_id` is indexed.
explain shows `totalDocsExamined: 0` — the strongest win.

slides.page_title: Compound Indexes and the Prefix Rule

blocks.title: Two More Truths
items: Non-prefix fields filter after the seek: IXSCAN, loose bounds.
Index intersection exists but rarely beats one compound index.
Design for query shapes: list your top queries first.
Direction matters only in compound indexes, relative to siblings.
`{a:1,b:-1}` serves `sort({a:1,b:-1})` — forward walk.
The same index serves `sort({a:-1,b:1})` — backward walk.
It does NOT serve `sort({a:1,b:1})`: one walk cannot flip one field.

blocks.title: The Inverse Test
blocks.text: A sort is index-supported when the requested pattern equals the index pattern or its exact inverse — every field flipped, none left alone.

items: Sort keys must form an index prefix, or follow equality fields.
`{status:1,createdAt:1}` plus `find({status:'A'})` sorts free.
Equality pins `status` constant, so `createdAt` acts as prefix.
`find({status:{$gt:'A'}})` absorbs nothing — blocking sort returns.

left.title: index sort
items: Streams the first doc instantly
`limit(10)` stops at 10 keys
No memory ceiling

right.title: blocking SORT
items: Buffers every result first
`limit(10)` gains nothing
100 MB cap, then error
Prefer range pagination on the sort key over `skip`.
`{createdAt: {$lt: lastSeen}}` reseeks instead of re-walking.
`allowDiskUse: true` spills a big sort — a bandage, not a fix.

blocks.title: Collation Note
items: An index built with one collation cannot serve another.
Mismatch kills both the sort and the equality match.

blocks.title: Never Trust `$natural`
blocks.text: `$natural` ignores indexes and returns storage order. It is not an ordering guarantee — never build semantics on top of it.

items: Index an array field and MongoDB makes it multikey automatically.
No option, no flag, no separate command to run.
One document produces N keys, one per array element.
All N keys point back to the same `RecordId`.
`find({tags:'mongo'})` seeks one key — membership is equality.
Index size tracks total array cardinality, not document count.
1M docs with 50-element arrays hold 50M index keys.
A compound index may hold at most ONE array-valued field.
Two arrays would demand a cartesian product of keys.
An insert making both arrays fails: `cannot index parallel arrays`.
The multikey flag is per-index and sticky — it survives the delete.

blocks.title: No Covered Queries
blocks.text: The multikey flag disables index-only plans. Expect a FETCH on every multikey hit, however tight the bounds look in explain.

items: The index narrows one condition; the other rechecks in FETCH.
So multikey bounds are looser than explain makes them look.

blocks.title: Subdocument Arrays
items: `createIndex({'items.sku':1})` indexes each element's `sku`.
One key per element, same RecordId, same limits apply.

lines: // only ONE text index per collection

items: An inverted-style index over tokenized, stemmed, filtered terms.
One text index per collection, but it may cover many fields.
`createIndex({'$**':'text'})` indexes every string field.
Wildcard text is cheap to type, expensive to run in production.
Terms are OR-ed by default; escaped quotes make a phrase.
A leading minus negates a term inside the same search string.
Score only via `{score:{$meta:'textScore'}}` in the projection.
Sort it with `sort({score:{$meta:'textScore'}})`.
Use `'none'` for codes, identifiers, non-linguistic tokens.
A text index is implicitly multikey — many term keys per doc.
It is often larger on disk than the data it indexes.
Cannot sit inside `$or` beside non-text clauses.
Cannot be negated with `$not`; one `$text` per query.
No prefix or substring match: `mongo` misses `mongodb`.
Compound text puts equality fields first, and the query must supply them.

blocks.title: Reach For Atlas Search
blocks.text: Substring, fuzzy matching and real relevance tuning need Lucene-backed Atlas Search. `$text` is the blunt self-hosted tool.

blocks.title: Defaults
items: Case and diacritic insensitive by default (version 3 indexes).
Toggle per query with `caseSensitive` / `diacriticSensitive`.
The field must be a BSON Date, or an array of Dates.
Any other type and the document simply never expires.
With an array of Dates the EARLIEST date decides expiry.
Still a normal single-field index: serves queries and sorts.
Deletion latency is up to ~60s plus the delete itself.
TTL deletes are real deletes: change streams fire, oplog grows.
A mass expiry is a write storm — spread your timestamps.
Runs on the primary only; secondaries apply replicated deletes.

blocks.title: Absolute Expiry
blocks.text: Set `expireAfterSeconds: 0` and store the exact desired deletion timestamp in the field. The monitor then honours your date verbatim.

caption.text: Your query is either seeking or scanning, and `explain` is the only thing that will tell you which. This field guide walks the whole index zoo — B-tree mechanics, the prefix rule, ESR field order, multikey array traps, TTL, text, and the planner mistakes that quietly turn a seek back into a COLLSCAN. Ten pages of dense notes: save it before your next slow-query hunt.
